Q: What is the system call interface? A:

The Linux syscall interface forwards system calls from programs to the OS kernel, where they are executed.

An Application Program Interface (API) is basically a set of specifications for source code to perform operations. People usually think of “the Linux system API” as the UNIX specification as documented and extended in section 3 of the Linux man pages, but there is also a non-portable, lower-level API to call system calls directly, and several others to call it from other languages, although many of these use their Foreign Function Interface (FFI) to call the C library.

So, programs will normally call open(), declared in unistd.h, and the compiler will link the call to a system library (historically called libc.so). On Linux, the implementation would normally call the syscall() function defined in syscall.h and sys/syscall.h with a value of SYS_open, defined as 2. In kernel mode, the kernel syscall interface is declared in asm/unistd.h, which defines the equivalent constant under the name __NR_open.

Which bytes and machine-language instructions this source code compiles to is an Application Binary Interface (ABI). This looks completely different on different hardware. On Linux x86-64, it sets a number of registers and then executes a syscall machine instruction to switch to kernel mode (ring 0, the kernel address space with its permissions, etc.).

Q: How to supply sample weights to Tensorflow dataset in R A:

The syntax you have used has the nested list which TensorFlow interprets as a single input group rather than three distinct components. In your code, you have list(list(inputs, targets, weights)) but you need list(inputs, targets, weights).

train_dataset <- tensor_slices_dataset(list(
  list("input_tensor" = image_data[!test_set,,,]), 
  list("output_tensor" = label_data[!test_set,]), 
  sample_weights[!test_set]
))

Q: -rpath-link=dir not able to locate the shared library A:

When linking libraries (-l(shared objects, or executables), the linker will use the following directories: (See man ld, or https://linux.die.net/man/1/ld - section about '-rpath-link'):

  1. Any directories specified by -rpath-link options.

  2. Any directories specified by -rpath options.

  3. if the -rpath and -rpath-link options were not used, directories included in the environment variable "LD_RUN_PATH".

  4. Directories included in the environment variable "LD_LIBRARY_PATH".

  5. The directories in "DT_RUNPATH" or "DT_RPATH" of a shared library are searched for shared libraries needed by it. The "DT_RPATH" entries are ignored if "DT_RUNPATH" entries exist.

  6. The default directories, normally /lib and /usr/lib.

  7. For a native linker on an ELF system, if the file /etc/ld.so.conf exists, the list of directories found in that file.

In this case:

  • libd is using rpath-link, which mean that he does not "REMEMBER" the reference to ../a (It's not stored in the shared-object DT_RUNPATH).

  • When linking the main program, the effective search path for liba includes only d (from the -L), and b (from the -rpath-link).

  • As indicated by rule 5 above - even if the libd link was modified to use 'rpath' - it will not change the search path for building the main program. The '../a' will only be used to search for shared objects DIRECTLY needed by libd, and will not help resolve the reference from libb to liba.

Bottom line - you have to provide search path for "a", when linking to "b", by

  • Providing -rpath/-rpath-link to "a" when linking the main program, OR

  • Providing -rpath to "a", when building "libb.so"

Q: Using NgxControlValueAccessor with [field] causes ERROR RuntimeError: NG0950: Input "field" is required but no value is available yet A:

It seems there's a timing problem between NgxControlValueAccessor and the new [field] directive.

[field] inputs are assigned after the directive is constructed, but NgxControlValueAccessor.initialValue() checks the control too soon.

This leads to NG0950 because the necessary field input isn't ready yet.

One solution is to wait to access cva.value$ / InteropNgControl until ngOnInit or afterNextRender.

In the long run, NgxControlValueAccessor should either postpone initialization or be able to handle missing initial values.
